diagnostic_evidence.quote: For any fixed extension $\delta > 0$, the growth is logarithmic.

It is a well-established result in approximation theory that the Lebesgue constant for polynomial interpolation at these nodes exhibits logarithmic growth (see, for example, \cite{brutman1996lebesgue, trefethen2019approximation}).
$|\sin\theta_j| \ge \sin(\theta_{\min}) = \sin\left(\frac{\pi\delta}{L+2\delta}\right) > 0$

issues.failure_explanation: For fixed $\delta>0$, $\theta_{\min}=\pi\delta/(L+2\delta)>0$ and $\theta_{\max}=\pi-\theta_{\min}<\pi$, so $|\sin\theta|\ge\sin\theta_{\min}>0$ on the whole collocation range. Hence consecutive nodes $\xi_k=\cos\theta_k$ differ in spacing by at most the constant factor $1/\sin\theta_{\min}$: they are quasi-equispaced on $[\cos\theta_{\max},\cos\theta_{\min}]$, not Chebyshev-clustered (clustering requires $\theta_{\min}=0$, i.e. $\delta=0$). Polynomial interpolation at quasi-equispaced nodes has exponentially growing Lebesgue constant (Runge/Ehlich-Zeller mechanism), so the cited log bound is invoked outside its hypotheses. By the paper's own identity $\ell_j(\theta)=\frac{\sin\theta}{\sin\theta_j}L_j(\cos\theta)$, $\Lambda_N\ge\sin\theta_{\min}\times$(polynomial Lebesgue constant at the $\xi$-nodes), so $\Lambda_N$ grows exponentially in $N$ for every fixed $\delta>0$ (equivalently, $N$ modes sampled at $N$ equispaced points on an arc of length $\pi L/(L+2\delta)$ have $\sim 2\delta N/(L+2\delta)$ unstable dimensions by Landau/prolate counting). A secondary slip: replacing $1/\sin(\theta_{\min})$ by $\cot(\theta_{\min})$ is invalid for large $\delta$ (where $\cot\to0$).

failure_location.quote: The nodes $\xi_j = \cos\theta_j$ are therefore cosines of equispaced angles. While not identical to classical Chebyshev points, such nodes exhibit the same characteristic clustering near the interval endpoints.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Withdraw the fixed-$\delta$ logarithmic claim (and thm:added-4), or re-scope it to regimes with $\delta=\delta(N)\to0$ or oversampled grids; no repair preserves the stated guarantee at square equispaced grids with fixed $\delta>0$.
issues.overall_effect: Theorem thm:basis_bound, its remark ('exceptionally well-behaved', 'near-optimal'), and the multidimensional version thm:added-4 ($O((\log N)^d)$) are unreliable: the true Lebesgue constant grows exponentially in $N$ for fixed $\delta$. The section 3.1 narrative that the basis itself is stable is false.
issues.title: Logarithmic Lebesgue bound for basis interpolation is false; growth is exponential for fixed delta
issues.why_classification: The stated guarantee (logarithmic growth for any fixed $\delta>0$) is false - the true growth is exponential - so the theorem and its dependent must be abandoned or re-scoped to a different regime; no comparable version survives in the stated setting.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: For a fixed number of basis functions $N \ge 3$, the Lebesgue constant $\Lambda_N$ for interpolation in the basis $\{w_j(x)\}$ is unbounded as the extension parameter $\delta \to \infty$.

This means the odd-indexed basis functions become nearly constant on $I$ (e.g., $w_1 \approx 1/\sqrt{\delta}$, $w_3 \approx -1/\sqrt{\delta} \approx -w_1$), while the even-indexed functions are nearly zero. The basis thus loses its ability to represent varied functions on $I$, and the interpolation problem becomes ill-posed.

issues.failure_explanation: The final inference is invalid: the Lebesgue constant is $\max_x\|W(\delta)^{-T}w(x)\|_1$, not $\|W^{-1}\|$, and the evaluation vectors $w(x)$ shrink at the same rate as the small singular values (the scaling cancels exactly: with $\tilde W=\sqrt{(L+2\delta)/2}\,W$ and $\tilde w(x)=\sqrt{(L+2\delta)/2}\,w(x)\to(\sin(j\pi/2))_j\ne0$, one has $W^{-T}w(x)=\tilde W^{-T}\tilde w(x)$). In fact the theorem is false. For $N=3$ with the uniform grid (nodes $\theta=\theta_m,\pi/2,\pi-\theta_m$, $\theta_m=\pi\delta/(L+2\delta)$), the exact cardinal functions satisfy, with $\tau=\pi(x-L/2)/(L+2\delta)$ and $\varepsilon=\pi L/(2(L+2\delta))\in(0,\pi/6]$, $|y_1+y_3|=|\cos\tau-\cos3\tau|/|\cos\varepsilon-\cos3\varepsilon|\le1$, $|y_1-y_3|=|\sin2\tau|/|\sin2\varepsilon|\le1$, $|y_2|\le2$, so $\Lambda_3(\delta)\le3$ for all large $\delta$, and $\Lambda_3(\delta)\to5/4$. Generally, for fixed $N$ the rescaled basis $\sqrt{(L+2\delta)/2}\,w_j(x)=\sin(j(\pi/2+\varepsilon\rho))$, $\rho=2(x-L/2)/L\in[-1,1]$, tends to a basis of $\Pi_{N-1}$ in $\rho$ (the even/odd blocks give nonsingular generalized Vandermonde matrices in $j^2$), and the interpolation operators converge in norm to degree-$(N-1)$ polynomial interpolation at the rescaled equispaced nodes, whose Lebesgue constant is a finite $N$-dependent constant. The rank-deficient limit matrix $M=\mathbf 1\mu^T$ does make the collocation matrix ill-conditioned in coefficient space, but not the Lebesgue constant.

failure_location.quote: The smallest singular value $\sigma_{\min}(\mat{W}(\delta))$ must tend to zero. The Lebesgue constant, which depends on the norm of the inverse of the collocation matrix, must therefore be unbounded as $\delta \to \infty$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Withdraw the theorem (the Lebesgue constant is bounded as $\delta\to\infty$, converging to a polynomial-interpolation constant); any replacement large-$\delta$ warning must be restated for a different quantity (e.g., the coefficient-space condition number of $W$ or the approximation power of $V_N$ on $I$), which is a different guarantee.
issues.overall_effect: Theorem thm:added-1 and the following remark (large-$\delta$ instability of the interpolation operator, 'the interpolation problem becomes ill-posed', 'This confirms that there is an optimal, problem-dependent value of $\delta$') are unreliable: the advertised instability of the interpolation operator as $\delta\to\infty$ does not exist.
issues.title: Claimed unboundedness of the Lebesgue constant as delta tends to infinity is false (it stays bounded)
issues.why_classification: The primary claim is false - the quantity stays bounded and converges to a finite limit - so no comparable version of the stated theorem survives; only a claim about a different quantity could replace it.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Since our basis functions are eigenfunctions of the Laplacian on the extended domain, this new basis is explicitly $\{\phi_j(x) = \lambda_j w_j(x)\}$.
The Lebesgue constant $\Lambda_N$ for interpolation in the space $V_N=\text{span}\{w_j\}_{j=1}^N$ is bounded by:

The stability of the extended-domain method for the Poisson equation presents a subtle dichotomy. The underlying basis functions $\{w_j\}$, which are pure sinusoids, exhibit near-optimal stability properties for interpolation.

It proves that the interpolation operator for the Poisson equation is unstable in the $L^\infty$ norm, a direct consequence of the $\lambda_j \propto j^2$ scaling introduced by the second-derivative operator.

issues.failure_explanation: Multiplying each basis function by the nonzero constant $\lambda_j$ does not change the interpolation space: $\Phi_N=\mathrm{span}\{\lambda_j w_j\}=\mathrm{span}\{w_j\}=V_N$. The Poisson-operator Lebesgue constant is therefore identically the basis-interpolation Lebesgue constant that thm:basis_bound bounds by $C\cot(\theta_{\min})\log N$ at the same uniform grid. The paper simultaneously asserts $O(\log N)$ (section 3.1) and super-polynomial growth (thm:added-2, section 3.2) for the same operator - an internal contradiction - and the advertised cause ('quadratic scaling of the eigenvalues', 'ill-conditioning of spectral differentiation' in the abstract) is mathematically vacuous: rescaling basis functions cannot change the interpolation operator. The (real) Poisson instability comes from the equispaced extended-domain sampling geometry (Runge/Landau mechanism), not from the $\lambda_j$ factors, and there is no basis-vs-operator stability dichotomy as claimed in section 3 and the 'Stability Dichotomy' remark.

failure_location.quote: The eigenvalues $\lambda_j \propto j^2$ introduce a quadratic scaling with the frequency index, which, as we now prove, catastrophically degrades the stability of the interpolation problem.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Retract the $\lambda_j$-scaling mechanism and the basis-versus-operator dichotomy; reattribute the Poisson instability to the extended-domain equispaced interpolation geometry and remove/rewrite the contradicting stability claim for the basis.
issues.overall_effect: The paper's central interpretive claim - a stability dichotomy in which the self-adjoint operator's eigenvalue scaling destabilizes an otherwise stable basis - is false; the abstract's and conclusion's causal accounts ('due to the ill-conditioning of spectral differentiation', 'The $j^2$ scaling ... induces a super-polynomial growth') are unreliable, and sections 3.1-3.2 make contradictory claims about the same quantity.
issues.title: False mechanism: the lambda_j ~ j^2 scaling cannot degrade the Lebesgue constant (Phi_N = V_N)
issues.why_classification: The repair is a correction of false causal/narrative prose with no additional formal-result loss beyond the separately reported defects, but it withdraws a central advertised insight, so it is more than minor.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: For fixed $L>0, \delta>0$, let $\theta_k(N) = \frac{N\pi}{L+2\delta}\left(\frac{kL}{N-1} + \delta\right)$.
The points $x_k = kL/(N-1)$ form a uniform grid.
We can assume without loss of generality that $\alpha$ is an irrational number.
The total error $\Delta_k = \frac{\theta_k(N)}{\pi} - m_k$ can be shown to be bounded by:
We state the result here and the proof is detailed in Appendix \ref{LemmaProof}

issues.failure_explanation: If all $|\sin\theta_k(N)|<\varepsilon$, then every consecutive spacing $\Delta_N=\theta_{k+1}(N)-\theta_k(N)=\pi NL/((L+2\delta)(N-1))=\pi\frac{N}{N-1}\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+1}$ (with $\alpha=L/(2\delta)$ fixed) must lie within $2\varepsilon/\pi$ of an integer. But for fixed $(L,\delta)$: if $0<\alpha<1$, $\mathrm{dist}(\Delta_N,\mathbb Z)\ge\min(\alpha,1-\alpha)/(\alpha+1)>0$ for all $N$; otherwise (non-integer $\alpha$, rational or irrational) $|\Delta_N-1|=|N-1-\alpha|/((N-1)(\alpha+1))\ge\mathrm{dist}(\alpha,\mathbb Z)/((N-1)(\alpha+1))=\Omega(1/N)$; for integer $\alpha$, $\Delta_N=1$ only at the single value $N=\alpha+1$, where the offset $\theta_0/\pi=1/(2\alpha)$ still gives $\max_k|\sin\theta_k|=\sin(\pi/(2\alpha))>0$. Hence $\max_k|\sin\theta_k(N)|\gtrsim c/N$ at best for all $N$: exponential decay along a subsequence is impossible for every fixed $(L,\delta)$, so the lemma is false. The appendix proof is also internally broken: the WLOG irrationality is illegitimate (and insufficient even for irrational $\alpha$ per the spacing obstruction), the integers $m_k$ are never defined, several derivations are abandoned mid-stream, and the decisive bound $|\Delta_k|\le C q_j|\epsilon_j|$ is asserted, not proven. Consequently thm:added-2's lower-bound mechanism yields at most $\Lambda_N\gtrsim O(N)$, and its proof collapses (the theorem's conclusion is in fact true via the Runge mechanism of ISSUE-001, but nothing in the source establishes it).

diagnostic_evidence.quote: $\int_{J_1} \sum_{j=1}^K |\ell_j(x)|^2 dx \le \frac{C_{\text{geom}}}{K}$
This degree-independent bound is a deep property of such interpolation schemes.
For analytical convenience, let these be Chebyshev-type points mapped to a subinterval $[a,b] \subset I$, for instance, $[L/4, 3L/4]$.
This shows that $\sigma_{\min}(A)$ is bounded below by a constant $C_{\min} > 0$, which is independent of $N$.

issues.failure_explanation: For any fixed $\delta>0$, degree-$M$ trigonometric polynomials can concentrate on the extension strips: by classical Remez/prolate (Slepian-Landau) theory the restriction map $P_M\to L^2(I)$ has smallest singular value $\asymp e^{-cM}$ (about $2\delta M/(L+2\delta)$ unstable dimensions), so $\sup_{g\in P_M}\|g\_{L^2(\tilde I)}/\|g\_{L^2(I)}$ grows like $e^{cM}$: no degree-independent $C_R$ exists. The failure extends to the very space used by thm:convdiff: writing $\theta=\pi(x+\delta)/(L+2\delta)$ and $K=k_0(L+2\delta)/\pi$, one checks $L[u_N]=C(K\sigma-\dot\sigma)$ where $\sigma$ ranges over cosine polynomials of degree $\le N$; taking $\sigma$ to be a near-best approximant of $e^{K(\theta-\pi/2)}$ on the arc $[\theta_{\min},\pi-\theta_{\min}]$ (geometric error $\rho^{-N}$, since $e^{K\arccos\xi}$ is analytic on $[-\cos\theta_{\min},\cos\theta_{\min}]$ with branch points only at $\xi=\pm1$) gives $\|L[u_N]\|_{L^2(I)}\lesssim\mathrm{poly}(N)\rho^{-N}\|L[u_N]\|_{L^2(\tilde I)}$, so the needed inequality fails exponentially even for $\{L[u_N]\}$, and $\sigma_{\min}$ of the convection-diffusion collocation matrix decays geometrically. The appendix proof is also broken: (i) the claim $\int_{J_1}\sum_j|\ell_j(x)|^2dx\le C_{\mathrm{geom}}/K$ for Chebyshev cardinal functions evaluated a fixed distance outside the node interval is exponentially false (they grow like $(|y|+\sqrt{y^2-1})^K$, e.g. $y=2$ at $x=0$ for $[a,b]=[L/4,3L/4]$, giving $\sim 13^K$); (ii) the Marcinkiewicz-Zygmund step uses $K$ nodes confined to $[L/4,3L/4]$ to control $\|g\|_{L^2(I)}$, which is impossible since $g$ can concentrate on $(0,L/4)\cup(3L/4,L)$.

issues.failure_explanation: Read for the containing space (trigonometric polynomials of degree $M=O(N)$, of dimension $2M+1>N$), the claim is false: the sampling map at $N$ points has a nontrivial kernel (dimension $\ge 2M+1-N$), and any nonzero kernel polynomial $T$ satisfies $\sum_i|T(x_i)|^2=0$ while $\|T\|_{L^2(I)}>0$ (a trigonometric polynomial cannot vanish on an interval), contradicting the inequality for every $c_1'>0$. Classical Marcinkiewicz-Zygmund inequalities require roughly $2M+1$ equispaced samples over a full period (or appropriately oversampled grids); they are invoked here outside their hypotheses ($N$ samples on the subinterval $I$). If instead the claim is restricted to the $N$-dimensional space $\Phi_N=\mathrm{span}\{L[u_N]\}$, it is exactly the discrete well-conditioning of the collocation matrix that thm:convdiff sets out to prove - i.e., the premise is circular and unestablished, and the cited reference does not cover this square, subinterval-collocation setting.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: the boundary value problem $-u'' + k(x)u' = f$ with homogeneous Dirichlet conditions
For a set of $N$ distinct collocation points $\{x_k\}_{k=1}^N \subset I$, the coefficients $\vect{c} = (c_1, \dots, c_N)^T$ are found by enforcing the PDE at these points:
The stated convergence rate then follows from the fundamental approximation properties of spectral methods for functions of finite Sobolev regularity.

For the unstable Poisson operator, direct computation of $\Lambda_N$ is difficult; we instead compute the condition number of the full boundary value problem matrix, which serves as a robust proxy for instability.

issues.failure_explanation: The proof establishes only the regularity premise $u\in H^{r+2}$ (standard elliptic theory, correct); the error bound for the method's solution $u_N$ does not follow. The method of Section 2 determines $\mathbf c$ from $N$ interior PDE collocation equations only - the Dirichlet conditions of the stated BVP are never enforced - so $u_N$ is not tied to the BVP solution: the implicit constraints (the basis vanishing at the extended boundary) select a different member of the 2-parameter solution family. For example, for $-u''=1$ on $(0,L)$ with $u(0)=u(L)=0$, the (formally stable) limit of the defined method on $I$ is $x(L-x)/2+\delta(L+\delta)/2$, whose value at $x=0$ is $\delta(L+\delta)/2\ne0$ for every fixed $\delta$: the $L^2$ error does not tend to zero, so the $O(N^{-(r+2)})$ claim is false for the method as defined. (Establishing the claim for a boundary-condition-enforced variant would additionally require the polynomial Lebesgue-constant stability, which is unproven or false elsewhere in the paper.) The numerical section confirms the implemented scheme differs from the analyzed one, since it uses 'the full boundary value problem matrix' and 'Dirichlet boundary data', objects absent from the Section 2 framework and from the analyzed matrix $A$.
